strengths: Clear conceptual extension of the probabilistic adversarial attack framework (Zhang et al. 2024) from single images to concept-level distributions, with a reasonably intuitive motivation (increasing overlap between pdis and pvic).
Provides both theoretical (Theorem 1 & 2) and empirical (KL divergence estimates across 26 concepts) support for the central claim that broadening pdis to a concept reduces divergence from pvic.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation: white-box and black-box transfer success rates, adversarially-trained defenses, no-reference image quality metrics, CLIP similarity, and a human user study.

Useful ablations, including sensitivity to the number of samples M and concept-set size |Cori|, and testing with multiple surrogate/victim architectures (ResNet50, MobileNetV2, ViT-Base) in the appendix.
Practical, reproducible pipeline for concept augmentation combining LoRA fine-tuning, SDXL, and GPT-4o prompting, which could be useful beyond this specific application.
Honest discussion of limitations (computational cost) and a practical usage guideline section.
weaknesses: The core novelty is somewhat incremental: it is largely a straightforward extension of an existing probabilistic attack framework (Zhang et al., 2024) to a multi-image/concept setting, with the underlying mechanism (fit a generative model to more data) not being conceptually new.

Theorem 1's assumptions (pdis and pvic modeled as Gaussians with matched means and pdis having higher variance) are a strong simplification that is not empirically validated for the actual high-dimensional diffusion-based distributions used in experiments; the theoretical result itself (KL decreasing in variance under a threshold) is a fairly generic and simple observation.

Potential confound in the main experiments: baselines (NCF, ACA, DiffAttack) do not benefit from the same generative augmentation/fine-tuning pipeline as the proposed method, so gains could partly stem from extra compute/data used to build the concept model rather than the 'concept' framing per se; the |Cori|=1 vs 30 ablation partially addresses this but is not the main comparison table.

Reporting transferability as top-100 success (rather than top-1) is non-standard and inflates apparent success rates, making results harder to interpret or compare to prior literature; very low top-1 white-box rates for some baselines (e.g., NCF 1.15%, ACA 6.03%) raise questions about baseline tuning/reproducibility.

Some quantitative results are inconsistent with the paper's narrative: e.g., NCF achieves the highest average CLIP similarity score in Table 2, undermining the claim that the proposed method best preserves the original concept by this metric.

The evaluation is limited to a small set of 26 DreamBooth concepts and 30 target classes; no comparison against a broader/standard adversarial robustness benchmark (e.g., RobustBench) or additional datasets.

The human user study is limited in scale (5 annotators, no inter-annotator agreement reported) and is only conducted for the main ResNet50 setting, not for the additional surrogate models in the appendix.

Practical scalability is questionable given the reported ~8 hours of diffusion fine-tuning per concept, which is only briefly acknowledged as a limitation without deeper discussion of mitigation strategies.

strengths: Natural and reasonably well-motivated extension of the probabilistic adversarial attack framework (Zhang et al. 2024) from single images to a 'concept' represented by a set of images or generative model.

The paper includes theoretical derivations (Theorems 1 and 2) attempting to formally justify why broadening the distance distribution to a concept should reduce KL divergence to the victim distribution, and backs this up with Monte-Carlo estimates across 26 concepts.

Fairly extensive empirical evaluation: multiple white-box surrogate models (ResNet50, MobileNetV2, ViT-Base), several black-box/transfer targets, adversarially-trained defenses, multiple no-reference image-quality metrics, CLIP similarity, and a human user study.
Useful and practical concept-augmentation pipeline (SDXL + LoRA + GPT-4o prompting) to expand small DreamBooth-style concept sets into more diverse training data for the distance distribution.
Reasonably thorough ablations (sample budget M, conservative vs. aggressive selection strategies) and an honest discussion of limitations (computational cost) and practical usage guidelines.
weaknesses: The core novelty is incremental: the paper largely reuses the probabilistic adversarial framework of Zhang et al. [49] and simply substitutes a multi-image/generative concept distribution for a single-image distance distribution; the main new technical contributions (data augmentation pipeline, sample-selection heuristics) are engineering rather than conceptual advances.

The comparison to baselines may be unfair: the proposed method is given substantially more information (an entire augmented concept set of up to 30 images and a fine-tuned generative model per concept) while baselines operate on a single image, so improved success/quality could simply reflect more data/compute rather than a fundamentally better attack principle.

Reported transferability is measured only via a relaxed 'top-100' criterion; the paper explicitly omits the actual top-1 black-box transfer numbers ('uniformly low across all methods') without ever reporting them, which obscures how practically effective the attack really is and undermines the strength of the headline results.

The threat model requiring an existing set of images of the *same specific object/identity* (and hours of per-concept diffusion-model fine-tuning, ~8 hours per concept on an H100) is a strong practical limitation that is only briefly acknowledged, substantially narrowing applicability relative to standard single-image adversarial-attack settings and raising questions about real-world relevance.

The theoretical results rely on a simplifying Gaussian/equal-mean assumption for the distance distributions that is not rigorously justified for real diffusion-model-based pdis, and Theorem 1 itself is a fairly elementary calculus result; the empirical KL-difference estimation (Appendix B) involves further heuristic corrections (pshare) whose validity is not carefully validated.

No comparison against simpler alternative baselines that could plausibly achieve similar gains without the 'concept' framing (e.g., ensembling single-image attacks across multiple images of the same object, or multi-crop/multi-augmentation attacks), making it hard to isolate the actual benefit of the proposed probabilistic concept formulation versus simply using more data.

The human user study is relatively small-scale (5 annotators) with no inter-annotator agreement reported, and was dropped entirely for the additional surrogate-model experiments (MobileNetV2, ViT-Base) due to cost, weakening the evidentiary basis for the concept-preservation claims in the broader experimental set.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated generalization of the probabilistic adversarial attack framework (Zhang et al.) from single images to concept-level distributions, with a clear mathematical bridge back to the single-image case as a special case.

Solid theoretical contribution: Theorem 1 shows KL divergence between pvic and a Gaussian pdis decreases with variance under reasonable conditions, and Theorem 2 provides a tractable expression for comparing KL divergences empirically, supported by rigorous proofs in the appendix.
Practical and creative pipeline for concept augmentation using LoRA fine-tuning of SDXL guided by GPT-4o generated prompts, addressing the real-world difficulty of obtaining diverse concept datasets.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: multiple baselines (NCF, ACA, DiffAttack, ProbAttack), multiple white-box surrogate models (ResNet50, MobileNetV2, ViT-Base), transferability across 5 standard and 3 adversarially-trained/ensemble classifiers.
Multi-faceted evaluation of concept/semantic preservation combining a user study, CLIP similarity, and six no-reference image quality metrics, going beyond simple attack success rate.
Useful ablation studies on sample count M and |Cori| size, clarifying trade-offs between conservative and aggressive sample-selection strategies.
Good reproducibility: detailed fine-tuning hyperparameters, compute resources, dataset/license information, and target class lists provided in appendices.
weaknesses: The evaluation scale is relatively limited (26 concepts x 30 target classes = 780 examples), which is modest for drawing strong general conclusions about attack efficacy across the full ImageNet label space.

Transferability is reported only via a lenient top-100 success criterion because top-1 transfer success was uniformly low for all methods; this weakens the practical significance of the claimed transferability gains and is an unconventional metric not clearly justified relative to the literature.

The comparison with baselines (ACA, DiffAttack, NCF, ProbAttack) may be somewhat unfair, since the proposed method leverages an additional 30 augmented images per concept (extra information/compute) that the single-image baselines do not have access to; a more information-matched baseline or ablation isolating the benefit of 'concept' information vs. simply more compute/data would strengthen the claims.

The theoretical analysis in Section 3.2 relies on a simplifying assumption (Gaussian pdis with identical mean but different variance for the single-image vs. concept case), which may not accurately reflect the behavior of diffusion-model-based pdis in practice; the empirical KL study in 3.3 is a reasonable but indirect validation.

The method is computationally expensive (per-concept diffusion model fine-tuning takes ~8 hours and SDXL LoRA fine-tuning ~20 minutes per concept), which the authors acknowledge as a limitation but do not quantify in terms of total cost relative to baselines.

The quality and diversity of the augmented concept dataset depends heavily on GPT-4o prompt generation and SDXL/LoRA fidelity, introducing an external dependency whose failure modes (e.g., concept drift during augmentation) are not analyzed.

The explicit distance D(xadv, Cori) is never formally defined, remaining implicit through the PGM; while this is acknowledged, it leaves the theoretical formulation somewhat underspecified for the concept case.

Ethical/security implications are discussed only briefly; given the paper explicitly aims to build more potent attacks that are 'exceedingly difficult to detect,' more discussion of defense strategies or responsible disclosure considerations would be valuable.

strengths: Extends the probabilistic adversarial attack framework (Zhang et al. 2024b) from single-image to concept-level distance distributions in a principled, mathematically consistent way, and is the first to explicitly target identity-level concept preservation (distinct from prior class-level unrestricted attacks).

Provides theoretical backing (Theorem 1 relating dispersion/temperature to KL divergence, Theorem 2 giving a tractable Monte Carlo estimator for the KL difference) that is empirically validated (∆̃ < 0 for all 26 concepts).

Extensive empirical evaluation across five different white-box victim classifiers (ResNet50, MobileNetV2, ViT-B, ConvNext, adversarially-trained ResNet50), multiple black-box transfer targets, multiple image-quality metrics, CLIP similarity, and a human user study.
Practical, well-documented pipeline for building diverse concept datasets via DreamBooth + SDXL LoRA + GPT-4o prompting, which is a useful engineering contribution beyond the core theoretical idea.

Good ablation studies (sample size M, |Cori| sensitivity, conservative vs aggressive sample selection) and honest discussion of limitations/trade-offs (e.g., transferability vs concept preservation trade-off in Appendix H).
Reasonable reproducibility effort: code, hyperparameters, dataset licensing, and compute resource details are provided.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is acknowledged by the authors themselves to be a fairly direct substitution (replacing xori with Cori in the existing padv formula); the theoretical results (Theorems 1-2) are relatively straightforward derivatives of standard KL divergence identities, limiting the depth of novelty.

Black-box transferability results remain very low in absolute terms (mostly single digits to low double digits in top-5/top-100), and the paper's own appendix concedes the method is far behind transferability-specialized methods, weakening the practical significance of the 'higher attack efficiency' claim.

The comparison across methods is inconsistent: the conservative selection strategy (OURS-CONS) frequently underperforms baselines like DiffAttack on transferability metrics, with only the aggressive strategy (OURS-AGGR) consistently winning, muddying the paper's overall narrative.

The approach requires building/curating a multi-image concept dataset and fine-tuning a diffusion model per concept (~8 hours per concept per Appendix I), a substantial overhead compared to single-image attacks; this practicality cost is understated in the main text's efficiency claims.

Evaluation is limited to a fairly narrow and small-scale benchmark (26-30 DreamBooth-style object/animal concepts), raising questions about generalizability to more complex or less object-centric 'concepts' (e.g., human identities, scenes, abstract categories).

The generated concept-augmentation pipeline itself relies on another generative model (SDXL+LoRA+GPT-4o), introducing potential confounds/biases into the 'concept distribution' and no ablation isolates the effect of augmentation quality versus the core method.

Given this work explicitly proposes a stronger, more evasive/harder-to-detect adversarial attack methodology with real-world attack scenarios (e.g., T-shirt patches, prohibited item evasion) described in the appendix, the defense/mitigation discussion is fairly shallow and largely deferred to future work.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and provides a coherent theoretical narrative connecting the proposed method to the existing probabilistic adversarial attack framework of Zhang et al. (2024b), including two KL-divergence theorems with proofs.

Extensive experimental protocol: multiple surrogate/white-box classifiers (ResNet50, MobileNetV2, ViT-Base, ConvNeXt, adversarially trained ResNet50), multiple black-box target models including adversarially trained/ensemble defenses, and several no-reference image-quality metrics plus a small user study.
The practical pipeline for building a diverse 'concept dataset' via DreamBooth + LoRA + SDXL + GPT-4o-generated prompts is a reasonable and reproducible engineering contribution.
Reasonably thorough ablations (sample budget M, |Cori| size) and an honest appendix discussion of the method's limited transferability compared to attacks explicitly designed for that purpose.
Reproducibility/ethics statements and code release intention are provided, along with a discussion of societal risks and mitigation strategies.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the core technical contribution is replacing a single image xori with a set/distribution Cori inside an already-published probabilistic adversarial framework (Zhang et al. 2024b); the paper itself concedes this is 'operationally a straightforward extension.' Theorem 1 is a fairly generic fact about Gibbs distributions and temperature/dispersion, not a deep new theoretical insight specific to adversarial attacks.

The threat/comparison setting is not apples-to-apples: the proposed method requires a curated multi-image (5-30 images) identity-level concept dataset and ~8 hours of diffusion fine-tuning per concept, whereas the single-image baselines (NCF, ACA, DiffAttack) need only seconds and a single input image. This large disparity in information and compute budget confounds the reported gains in success rate and image quality, making the comparison to single-image baselines questionable.

Despite the claimed improvement, absolute black-box transferability remains very low across the board (mostly single-digit top-5/top-10 percentages), and the appendix explicitly acknowledges that methods designed for transferability substantially outperform this approach — undermining the practical significance of the proposed attack.

The sample-selection procedure (drawing M=10 candidates and picking the 'best' via conservative/aggressive softmax-based heuristics) effectively performs best-of-N cherry-picking; it is unclear whether this advantage is applied symmetrically to all baselines, and the ad hoc, hand-designed selection heuristics feel unprincipled relative to the paper's ostensibly rigorous probabilistic framing.

The user study is very small-scale (5 annotators) and reported only for the ResNet50 setting due to cost, with no details on sample size per condition, inter-annotator agreement, or statistical testing — insufficient support for the claimed concept-preservation superiority.

The notion of 'concept' remains vague and subjective (acknowledged by the authors), and the practical requirement of possessing/curating a diverse image set of the exact same identity substantially narrows real-world applicability compared to standard single-image adversarial threat models.

The choice of a less powerful/appropriate base diffusion model (guided diffusion instead of SDXL/DDIM latent space used by the strongest baselines ACA/DiffAttack) could further bias quality/success comparisons, and this choice is only justified qualitatively ('more principled') rather than empirically validated.
Given the explicit example scenario of evading moderation for prohibited-item advertisements, the dual-use/ethical framing feels somewhat under-addressed beyond generic mitigation suggestions.

Overall, the empirical gains appear largely attributable to additional information (many images of the same identity) and vastly more compute rather than a fundamentally novel or more efficient attack mechanism, which limits the paper's contribution and significance for a top-tier venue.

strengths: Clean and well-motivated theoretical extension of the probabilistic adversarial attack framework (Zhang et al. 2024b) from single-image to concept-level distance distributions, supported by two theorems (KL divergence behavior with dispersion, and a tractable difference-of-KL estimator).
Empirical validation of the theory: Monte Carlo estimation of ΔKL confirms Δ<0 for all 26 tested concepts, directly supporting the core hypothesis.

Comprehensive experimental suite: results across 5 different white-box surrogate classifiers (ResNet50, MobileNetV2, ViT-Base, ConvNeXt, adversarially-trained ResNet50), multiple black-box/transfer targets and defenses, plus quantitative (CLIP score, six no-reference IQA metrics) and human user-study evaluation of concept preservation.

Well-designed ablations: ProbAttack serves as a principled special-case baseline (|Cori|=1), and a sensitivity study over M and |Cori| helps disentangle gains from sample selection vs. concept breadth.
Practical and reproducible concept-augmentation pipeline (SDXL+LoRA+GPT-4o) addressing the real bottleneck of obtaining diverse per-concept image sets.
Clear positioning relative to prior unrestricted/class-level/single-image attacks (Table 3), along with thorough reproducibility, ethics, and limitations discussions.
weaknesses: Core methodological novelty is limited: the extension amounts to replacing xori with Cori in an existing formulation, which the authors themselves describe as operationally straightforward; the added value rests substantially on engineering (data augmentation) rather than new theory.

High computational cost (~8 hours per concept for diffusion fine-tuning on an H100) versus baselines that take seconds-minutes, limiting practicality and scalability despite lower per-sample generation overhead.

Absolute black-box transferability remains low in absolute terms even though it beats baselines relatively; the paper's own appendix admits it cannot compete with attacks explicitly optimized for transferability, a caveat somewhat underemphasized in the main text/abstract framing of 'higher attack efficiency.'
Evaluation scope is narrow: single dataset (DreamBooth, 26 objects), single domain (ImageNet natural images), and identity-level concepts only; generality to other domains/concept types is untested.

Fairness of baseline comparison is not fully clear, since compared methods (NCF, ACA, DiffAttack) were originally designed more for untargeted/single-image settings and hyperparameter tuning for the harder targeted setting is not deeply justified.
Heavy reliance on appendices for essential results and details (full tables spanning many pages) makes the main text feel incomplete without extensive appendix reading.
